overview.title: Why activations are needed; deep learning as geometric transformation
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.subsection: 2.3.6 A geometric interpretation of deep learning
overview.main_topic: Composition of affine transforms collapses to one affine transform, so Dense layers need nonlinear activations; a neural network as a chain of simple geometric transformations in a high-dimensional space
overview.central_idea: Two affine transforms composed are still one affine transform (`(W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2)`), so a stack of `Dense` layers without activations is just a linear model in disguise; activation functions like `relu` break this and let chains of layers implement complex nonlinear transforms. A whole network is therefore a complex geometric transformation built from simple steps.
overview.importance: This page answers one of the most common beginner questions — why do layers need activation functions? — with a one-line algebraic proof and a picture (Figure 2.13). It then opens section 2.3.6, whose crumpled-paper image is the book's central mental model of what deep learning does, reused as late as the conclusions chapter (p.622).
learning_objectives: Show algebraically that composing two affine transforms yields an affine transform, identifying its linear and translation parts.
Explain why a multilayer network of Dense layers without activations is equivalent to a single Dense layer (a linear model).
Describe the geometric effect of relu after an affine transform (Figure 2.13) and why it makes rich, nonlinear hypothesis spaces possible.
Articulate the view of a neural network as a complex geometric transformation in high-dimensional space composed of simple steps, and begin the crumpled-paper analogy.
prerequisites: Affine transform = linear transform + translation, and Dense without activation = affine layer (p.61)

summary:
The page opens with Figure 2.12, which shows an affine transform `W • x + b` in the plane turning the square K into a sheared, shifted parallelogram.

The main bullet, *Dense layer with relu activation*, makes an important observation: applying many affine transforms in a row still yields an affine transform. With two of them, `affine2(affine1(x)) = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2)` — an affine transform whose linear part is the matrix `W2 @ W1` and whose translation part is the vector `W2 @ b1 + b2`. Consequently a multilayer network made entirely of `Dense` layers *without activations* would be equivalent to a single `Dense` layer: a 'deep' network that is just a linear model in disguise. This is why activation functions such as `relu` are needed. Figure 2.13 shows `relu(W • x + b)`: the same parallelogram, but with the part below the x-axis clipped off, a non-affine result. Thanks to activations, a chain of `Dense` layers can implement very complex, nonlinear geometric transformations, giving deep networks very rich hypothesis spaces (developed further in the next chapter).

Section 2.3.6, *A geometric interpretation of deep learning*, then draws the conclusion of the whole section: neural networks consist entirely of chains of tensor operations, each a simple geometric transformation of the input data, so a neural network can be read as one very complex geometric transformation in a high-dimensional space, implemented as a series of simple steps.

The final paragraph begins a 3-D mental image: take a red sheet and a blue sheet of paper, lay one on the other, and crumple them together into a ball. The ball is the input data; each sheet is one class of a classification problem. What the network has to do (continued on p.63) is figure out a transformation that uncrumples the ball so the classes become cleanly separable again.

paragraphs.excerpt: Dense layer with relu activation—An important observation about affine transforms is
paragraphs.what_it_says: Composing affine transforms gives another affine transform. With two: `affine2(affine1(x)) = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2)`, whose linear part is `W2 @ W1` and translation part is `W2 @ b1 + b2`. Hence a network built only from `Dense` layers without activations equals a single `Dense` layer — 'a linear model in disguise'. That is why activation functions like `relu` (Figure 2.13) are needed: with them, a chain of `Dense` layers implements very complex nonlinear transformations and gives rich hypothesis spaces. More in the next chapter.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The algebra is just distributing W2 over the sum and regrouping: `W2 @ (W1 @ x) = (W2 @ W1) @ x` (matrix products are associative) and `W2 @ b1 + b2` is a fixed vector. The result has exactly the `W @ x + b` form of p.61, with `W = W2 @ W1` and `b = W2 @ b1 + b2`. The same argument repeats for any number of layers, so depth buys nothing without a nonlinearity between layers. `relu` is applied element-wise and clips every negative coordinate to 0 — an operation that cannot be written as a matrix product plus a vector, which breaks the collapse.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the reason activation functions exist. Without this page the `activation="relu"` argument in the MNIST model (p.52) looks arbitrary; with it, you see that removing the activations would reduce the two-layer model to one affine map from 784 pixels to 10 classes, no matter how many hidden units you add.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The set of affine maps is closed under composition (it forms a group when W is invertible). Element-wise nonlinearities like relu are not affine, so interleaving them with affine maps escapes that closed set. Geometrically, Figure 2.13 shows relu 'folding' the plane: every point with a negative coordinate is projected onto the nearest axis, flattening part of the shape.

terminology.meaning: A deep stack of activation-free Dense layers: it has many parameters but can only represent a single affine map.
An element-wise nonlinear function (relu here) applied after the affine part of a layer so that stacked layers do not collapse.
The set of all functions a model could represent; activations make the hypothesis space of a chain of Dense layers much richer than that of a single affine map.

connections: p.61: affine transform defined as linear transform + translation; Dense without activation is affine.
p.53: relu(x) = max(x, 0) as the third operation of a Dense layer.
p.57: matmul is not symmetric — note the order W2 @ W1, not W1 @ W2.
p.133: chapter 4 returns to 'What are activation functions, and why are they necessary?'.

paragraphs.excerpt: You just learned that neural networks consist entirely of chains of tensor
paragraphs.what_it_says: Neural networks consist entirely of chains of tensor operations, and all of these are simple geometric transformations of the input data. Therefore a neural network can be interpreted as a very complex geometric transformation in a high-dimensional space, implemented as a series of simple steps.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the synthesis of section 2.3. Each layer is matmul (rotate/scale/shear), addition (translate), and an activation (fold). Chain enough of them and you get a transformation that no single step could produce, acting on points in a space whose dimension equals the number of input features (784 for MNIST).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a unified way to think about any network, regardless of architecture: 'what geometric transformation is this layer applying to the data, and what does the whole chain achieve?' The authors return to this view in the conclusions (p.622).
paragraphs.technical_idea: The network is a composition f = f_L ∘ … ∘ f_1 of simple differentiable maps; the 'high-dimensional space' is R^n with n the input size, and each layer maps between spaces of possibly different dimension.

terminology.meaning: A map that moves points in a space — rotation, scaling, translation, folding — here applied to data points.
The space whose coordinates are the input features; an MNIST image is a point in a 784-dimensional space.

connections: p.52: 'all transformations learned by deep neural networks can be reduced to a handful of tensor operations'.
p.59–61: the geometric readings of addition and matmul that this paragraph summarizes.
p.622: the conclusions chapter restates deep learning as 'turning meaning into vectors, into geometric spaces'.

paragraphs.excerpt: In 3D, the following mental image may prove useful. Imagine two sheets
paragraphs.what_it_says: A 3-D mental image: put a red sheet of paper on a blue one and crumple them together into a small ball. The ball is the input data; each sheet is one class in a classification problem. What a neural network must do is figure out (continued on p.63) a transformation that uncrumples the ball so the two classes become cleanly separable.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Real data of different classes is not neatly separated in input space — the classes are intertwined like the two crumpled sheets. A network's job is to find a geometric transformation that disentangles them, after which a simple decision (which sheet is this point on?) becomes easy.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This picture is the book's central intuition for *why* deep learning works: uncrumpling is done with many small finger movements, exactly as a deep network applies many simple layers. It also previews the notion of a data manifold (p.63).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Each class occupies a curved, folded surface (a manifold) inside the input space; a good representation is one where the manifolds are flattened and pulled apart so that a simple classifier (e.g. the final softmax layer) can separate them.

terminology.meaning: One of the categories to be predicted in a classification problem; one sheet of paper in the image.
Classes are separable when a simple boundary can be drawn between them — the goal of uncrumpling.

connections: p.63: Figure 2.14 'Uncrumpling a complicated manifold of data' and the definition of a manifold.
p.622: the same paper-ball image used in the conclusions.

concepts.name: Composition of affine transforms
concepts.definition: Applying one affine transform after another yields a single affine transform: W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2).
concepts.intuition: Turn-stretch-shift followed by turn-stretch-shift is just one bigger turn-stretch-shift; you could have done it in one go.
concepts.technical: Uses associativity of matmul and distributivity over addition. The combined linear part is the product of the matrices (in order W2 @ W1), the combined translation is W2 @ b1 + b2. Extends by induction to any number of affine maps.
concepts.significance: Proves that depth without nonlinearity adds no expressive power: a stack of activation-free Dense layers is 'a linear model in disguise'.
concepts.misconception: That the combined matrix is W1 @ W2 — matmul is not commutative (p.57); the later layer's matrix goes on the left.

concepts.name: Activation function (why it is necessary)
concepts.definition: A nonlinear function, applied element-wise after a layer's affine computation, that prevents stacked Dense layers from collapsing into a single affine map.
concepts.intuition: Affine maps can turn, stretch and shift a sheet but never bend it. The activation is what folds the sheet, so that a chain of layers can make shapes a single layer cannot.
concepts.technical: relu(x) = max(x, 0) is piecewise linear but not affine: it has no representation as W @ x + b. Interleaving it with affine layers makes the composition a nonlinear function whose complexity grows with depth.
concepts.significance: Without activations, 'this deep neural network would just be a linear model in disguise'. With them, a chain of Dense layers has 'very rich hypothesis spaces'.
concepts.example: In Figure 2.13, relu(W • x + b) keeps the parallelogram above the x-axis but flattens everything below it onto the axis — a result no affine map could produce from the square K.
concepts.misconception: That activations are only there to squash values into a range; their essential role is to introduce nonlinearity between layers.

concepts.name: relu
concepts.definition: relu(x) = max(x, 0), applied element-wise (p.53); geometrically it clips every negative coordinate to zero.
concepts.intuition: A one-way gate: positive values pass unchanged, negative values become 0.
concepts.technical: Piecewise linear with slope 1 for x > 0 and 0 for x < 0. Applied to a vector it projects any point outside the non-negative orthant onto its boundary, which is what makes the lower part of the shape in Figure 2.13 disappear.
concepts.significance: The activation the book uses in the MNIST model and the example of a nonlinearity that rescues depth.
concepts.misconception: That relu is linear because its graph is made of straight pieces — it is not: relu(−1) + relu(1) = 1 but relu(−1 + 1) = 0, violating additivity.

concepts.name: Deep learning as geometric transformation
concepts.definition: A neural network is a chain of simple geometric transformations (tensor operations) that together implement a very complex geometric transformation of the input data in a high-dimensional space.
concepts.intuition: Each layer nudges the cloud of data points a little; many nudges in sequence can reshape it drastically.
concepts.technical: f = f_L ∘ … ∘ f_1 where each f_i is an affine map followed by an element-wise nonlinearity; the data lives in R^n with n equal to the number of input features.
concepts.significance: The unifying view of section 2.3; the conclusions chapter (p.622) restates it as the 'magic of deep learning'.
concepts.example: The MNIST model maps 784-dimensional pixel vectors through a 512-dimensional space to a 10-dimensional output, one affine-plus-relu step at a time.
concepts.misconception: That 'geometric' means the network is restricted to rotations and scalings — the activation functions make the overall transformation highly nonlinear.

concepts.name: The crumpled-paper image
concepts.definition: Two sheets of coloured paper (two classes) crumpled together into a ball (the input data); the network must find a transformation that uncrumples them so the classes are cleanly separable.
concepts.intuition: Classes are tangled in input space; learning means untangling them with a sequence of simple moves.
concepts.technical: Each sheet is a low-dimensional manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space; a good representation flattens and separates these manifolds (continued on p.63).
concepts.significance: The book's central mental model for what deep networks do and why depth helps (many small uncrumpling steps).
concepts.example: Images of 3s and 8s are mixed together in pixel space; after the hidden layer's transformation they should occupy distinct, easily separated regions.
concepts.misconception: That the ball represents a single sample — it represents the whole dataset, with each sheet a class.

math.title: Two affine transforms compose into one affine transform
math.latex: \begin{aligned} \text{affine}_2(\text{affine}_1(x)) &= W_2 (W_1 x + b_1) + b_2 \\ &= (W_2 W_1)\, x + (W_2 b_1 + b_2) \end{aligned}
math.source_text: affine2(affine1(x)) = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2)

variables.meaning: Weight matrix and bias vector of the first affine layer.
Weight matrix and bias vector of the second affine layer.
The linear part of the composed transform (matrix product, in this order).
The translation part of the composed transform (a fixed vector).

math.operations: Distribute W2 over the sum (W2 @ (A + B) = W2 @ A + W2 @ B), use associativity of matmul (W2 @ (W1 @ x) = (W2 @ W1) @ x), then group the constant terms.
math.purpose: Shows that a stack of Dense layers without activations is equivalent to a single Dense layer — a linear model in disguise — and so motivates activation functions.
math.interpretation: The composed map has exactly the form W @ x + b with W = W2 @ W1 and b = W2 @ b1 + b2. Nothing about it is 'deeper' than a single layer; the extra parameters are redundant.
math.intuition: Shift-and-deform twice is one shift-and-deform. Only a non-affine step (a fold such as relu) can escape this.

math.title: Affine transform followed by relu (Figures 2.12 and 2.13)
math.source_text: Figure 2.12 label: W • x + b; Figure 2.13 label: relu(W • x + b)

variables.meaning: The affine part: linear transform W then translation b (Figure 2.12).
Element-wise max with 0 (defined on p.53), applied to each coordinate of the transformed point.
The output point; any negative coordinate has been clipped to 0 (Figure 2.13).

math.operations: Matrix product, vector addition, then element-wise clipping.
math.purpose: Shows what a Dense layer with relu does geometrically and why the result is no longer affine.
math.interpretation: In Figure 2.12 the square K becomes a parallelogram (shear + shift). In Figure 2.13 the part of that parallelogram below the x-axis is flattened onto the axis: relu sends every point with y < 0 to y = 0 (and every point with x < 0 to x = 0). Straight lines are kinked, so the map is nonlinear.
math.intuition: Fold the sheet along the axes so nothing hangs into the negative region.
math.numerical_example: If W @ x + b = [1.5, −0.8] then relu gives [1.5, 0]; if it is [−0.3, 2] the output is [0, 2]; a point already in the positive quadrant, [0.7, 0.4], is unchanged.

math.title: Generalization to L activation-free layers (not in the book)
math.latex: W_L(\cdots(W_1 x + b_1)\cdots) + b_L = \underbrace{(W_L \cdots W_1)}_{W}\, x + \underbrace{\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{L} W_L \cdots W_{k+1}\, b_k\Big)}_{b}
math.source_text: The book states the result in words ('if you apply many of them repeatedly, you still end up with an affine transform') and works out only the two-layer case.

variables.meaning: Weights and bias of layer k.
Collapsed linear part: the product of all matrices, last layer leftmost.
Collapsed translation: each b_k pushed through all later matrices, summed.

math.operations: Repeated application of the two-layer identity m1, by induction on L.
math.purpose: Makes explicit the book's claim that any number of activation-free Dense layers equals one Dense layer.
math.interpretation: No matter how many layers, the output is a single affine map of the input; the apparent depth is an illusion.
math.intuition: Each extra layer just multiplies the current matrix by another matrix and shifts the current offset.
math.numerical_example: For L = 2 the sum has two terms: W2 @ b1 (k = 1) and b2 (k = 2, empty product), recovering W2 @ b1 + b2 from the book.

deeper.title: Collapsing a two-layer activation-free network, step by step
deeper.body:
Start with the book's expression and do one algebraic move per line.

1. `affine2(affine1(x)) = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2` — substitute the first layer's output into the second.
2. `= W2 @ (W1 @ x) + W2 @ b1 + b2` — distribute `W2 @` over the sum.
3. `= (W2 @ W1) @ x + W2 @ b1 + b2` — regroup the matrix product (associativity).
4. `= (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2)` — collect the terms that do not depend on x.

Line 4 is `W @ x + b` with `W = W2 @ W1` and `b = W2 @ b1 + b2`: a single affine layer. For the MNIST model (p.52) without activations this would mean a 784 × 512 matrix times a 512 × 10 matrix collapsing to a single 784 × 10 matrix — the 512 hidden units contribute nothing that a one-layer model could not do.

Now insert `relu` between the layers: `W2 @ relu(W1 @ x + b1) + b2`. Step 2 is no longer possible, because `relu` of a sum is not the sum of `relu`s. The collapse is blocked, and the network can represent functions a single affine layer cannot.

deeper.title: Reading Figure 2.13: where did the bottom of the K go?
deeper.body:
Figure 2.12 shows the K after `W • x + b`: it has been sheared into a parallelogram that straddles the x-axis — part of it is above the axis and part below.

Figure 2.13 applies `relu` to every point of that parallelogram. `relu` acts coordinate by coordinate: any point with a negative y is moved straight up to y = 0, and any point with a negative x is moved right to x = 0. So the whole region of the parallelogram that was below the axis is squashed flat onto the axis, which is why the shape now has a straight bottom edge sitting exactly on the x-axis while its upper edge is unchanged.

This flattening is the geometric meaning of 'nonlinear': a straight line crossing the axis is bent into two segments. No matrix product plus translation can do that, so a layer with `relu` escapes the affine collapse proven in the text.

deeper.title: The paper ball and the finger movements
deeper.body:
Think of the dataset as thousands of points, half drawn on a red sheet, half on a blue one, and the two sheets crumpled together. In input space (pixel space for images) the red and blue points are hopelessly intermingled — there is no simple surface that separates them.

Each layer of the network is one small movement of your fingers: a little pull here, a little flattening there (an affine deformation plus a fold from the activation). None of the movements alone uncrumples the ball, but a long sequence of them, each chosen by training, can. At the end, the red sheet and the blue sheet lie flat and apart, and the final layer only needs to draw a straight boundary between them.

The analogy also explains why depth helps: an expert uncrumpling a ball uses many small gestures, not one magical motion. The book makes this explicit on p.63.

deeper.title: Try it in Keras (illustrative, not from the book)
deeper.body:
A quick empirical check of the page's claim: build two models on MNIST, one with `activation=None` in the hidden layer and one with `relu`.

```python
import keras
from keras import layers

def make(activation):
    return keras.Sequential([
        layers.Dense(512, activation=activation),
        layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
    ])

linear_in_disguise = make(None)   # two affine layers -> one affine map, then softmax
nonlinear = make("relu")
```

The first model, despite its 512 hidden units, can only learn the same decision boundaries as a single `Dense(10, activation="softmax")` layer (a multinomial logistic regression); the second can learn much more. Note that the final `softmax` is itself a nonlinearity, but it is applied after the collapse and only normalizes the outputs — it does not restore the lost expressive power of the hidden layer.

misconceptions.claim: Adding more Dense layers always makes a network more expressive.
misconceptions.correction: Only if there are nonlinear activations between them. The page shows that any number of activation-free Dense layers equals a single Dense layer: 'a linear model in disguise'.

misconceptions.claim: The combined matrix of two stacked layers is W1 @ W2.
misconceptions.correction: It is W2 @ W1 — the later layer's matrix multiplies on the left, because W2 is applied to the output of W1. Matmul is not commutative (p.57).

misconceptions.claim: relu is linear because its graph consists of straight lines.
misconceptions.correction: It is piecewise linear with a kink at 0, which is enough to break linearity: relu(a + b) ≠ relu(a) + relu(b) in general. Figure 2.13 shows the effect — part of the shape is flattened, something no linear or affine map can do.

misconceptions.claim: The crumpled paper ball in the analogy is one input sample.
misconceptions.correction: The ball is the entire input dataset; each sheet of paper is one class. The network's job is a transformation that separates the sheets, not a prediction for a single point.

takeaways: Two affine transforms compose into one: W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2) — linear part W2 @ W1, translation W2 @ b1 + b2.
Therefore a network of Dense layers without activations is equivalent to a single Dense layer: a linear model in disguise.
Activation functions such as relu break this collapse (Figure 2.13 shows relu flattening part of the transformed shape) and give chains of Dense layers rich, nonlinear hypothesis spaces.
A neural network is a very complex geometric transformation of the input data in a high-dimensional space, built from simple tensor-operation steps.
Mental image: two sheets of paper (classes) crumpled into a ball (the data); the network must uncrumple them so the classes become separable.

questions.question: Simplify affine2(affine1(x)) = W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 into the form W @ x + b, and state W and b.
questions.explanation: Distribute W2 over the sum and regroup the product by associativity: W2 @ (W1 @ x) = (W2 @ W1) @ x. The remaining terms W2 @ b1 + b2 do not depend on x and form the translation. This is exactly the derivation on the page.

questions.question: According to the page, what is a multilayer network made entirely of Dense layers without activation functions equivalent to?
options: A single Dense layer (a linear model in disguise)
A network with the same number of relu layers
A model that cannot be trained by gradient descent
questions.answer: A single Dense layer (a linear model in disguise)
questions.explanation: Because affine transforms compose into an affine transform, the stack equals one affine layer. The other options are not claimed: relu layers would be strictly more expressive, affine stacks are perfectly trainable (just not more expressive), and convolution is not mentioned here.

questions.question: Why does inserting relu between two Dense layers prevent the collapse into a single affine transform?
questions.answer: relu is not an affine map (it clips negative coordinates to 0, a nonlinear, element-wise operation), so W2 @ relu(W1 @ x + b1) + b2 cannot be rewritten as a single W @ x + b. The distributive step of the proof fails because relu of a sum is not the sum of relus.
questions.explanation: The page says activation functions like relu are needed precisely because they let a chain of Dense layers implement complex nonlinear transformations. Figure 2.13 shows the geometric effect: part of the transformed shape is flattened, which no matrix product plus translation can do.

questions.question: Describe what Figure 2.13 shows and how it differs from Figure 2.12.
questions.answer: Figure 2.12 shows the K after an affine transform W • x + b: a sheared, shifted parallelogram partly below the x-axis. Figure 2.13 applies relu to that result: the portion below the axis is clipped flat onto the axis, giving a straight bottom edge — the transform is no longer affine.
questions.explanation: relu(W • x + b) replaces every negative coordinate by 0, so points under the x-axis move up onto it. The difference between the two figures is exactly the nonlinearity the text says is required.

questions.question: In the crumpled-paper image begun on this page, what do the two sheets of coloured paper represent?
options: The two classes of a classification problem
The training set and the test set
The weights W and the biases b of a layer
The input and output of a single layer
questions.answer: The two classes of a classification problem

The page says a neural network can be interpreted as 'a very complex geometric transformation in a high-dimensional space, implemented via a series of simple steps'. What are the simple steps, and what is the high-dimensional space for the MNIST model of p.52?
questions.answer: The simple steps are the tensor operations of each layer — matmul (rotation/scaling/shear), vector addition (translation), and the activation (relu, a fold). For MNIST the input space is 784-dimensional (one coordinate per pixel); the first Dense layer maps it to a 512-dimensional space and the second to 10 dimensions.
questions.explanation: The paragraph summarizes section 2.3: every tensor operation has a geometric meaning (p.59–61), and layers chain them. The MNIST shapes come from the model in section 2.1 (p.52: Dense(512, activation="relu") followed by Dense(10)).

questions.question: Can you explain to a colleague, in under a minute and without notes, why 'a deep network without activations is a linear model in disguise'?
questions.answer: Each layer is W @ x + b. Feeding one into the next gives W2 @ (W1 @ x + b1) + b2 = (W2 @ W1) @ x + (W2 @ b1 + b2), again of the form W @ x + b. Repeat for any depth: still one affine map. An activation such as relu is nonlinear, so it stops this regrouping and lets depth add expressive power.
